claim: DNA replication in E. coli occurs at speeds of 600-1000 nucleotides per second.
source: In Escherichia coli, DNA replication is highly efficient with speeds of up 600–1000 nucleotides per second (Mok and Marians, 1987; Mcinerney et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to Mok and Marians, 1987 and Mcinerney et al., 2007

claim: E. coli DNA replication synthesizes >100,000 basepairs per binding event.
source: In Escherichia coli, DNA replication is highly efficient with speeds of up 600–1000 nucleotides per second (Mok and Marians, 1987; Mcinerney et al., 2007), >100,000 basepairs (bp) synthesized per binding event (Yao et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yao et al., 2009

claim: E. coli DNA replication has an error rate of approximately 1 per million.
source: In Escherichia coli, DNA replication is highly efficient with speeds of up 600–1000 nucleotides per second (Mok and Marians, 1987; Mcinerney et al., 2007), >100,000 basepairs (bp) synthesized per binding event (Yao et al., 2009), and an error rate of ∼1 per million (Bloom et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bloom et al., 1997

claim: The DNA polymerase III holoenzyme synthesizes the leading strand continuously.
source: To do so, DNA replication is performed by a large multi-protein complex termed the DNA polymerase III holoenzyme that synthesizes the leading strand in a continuous manner, while the lagging strand is synthesized in short fragments of ∼1000 bp.
evidence: Stated as a known property of the holoenzyme

claim: The lagging strand is synthesized in short fragments of approximately 1000 bp.
source: To do so, DNA replication is performed by a large multi-protein complex termed the DNA polymerase III holoenzyme that synthesizes the leading strand in a continuous manner, while the lagging strand is synthesized in short fragments of ∼1000 bp.
evidence: Stated as a known property of lagging strand synthesis

claim: The holoenzyme is composed of 10 subunits (α, β, ε, θ, δ, δ', γ, τ, χ, ψ).
source: The holoenzyme is composed of 10 subunits (α, β, ε, θ, δ, δ', γ, τ, χ, ψ), that together with the helicase DnaB and the RNA primase DnaG form the replisome with a combined molecular weight of 1 MDa.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about the holoenzyme composition

claim: The replisome has a combined molecular weight of 1 MDa.
source: The holoenzyme is composed of 10 subunits (α, β, ε, θ, δ, δ', γ, τ, χ, ψ), that together with the helicase DnaB and the RNA primase DnaG form the replisome with a combined molecular weight of 1 MDa.
evidence: Stated as a known property of the replisome

claim: The helicase DnaB separates the two DNA strands.
source: The helicase DnaB separates the two DNA strands (Mok and Marians, 1987)
evidence: Supported by citation to Mok and Marians, 1987

claim: DnaB transiently associates with the RNA primase DnaG.
source: The helicase DnaB separates the two DNA strands (Mok and Marians, 1987) and transiently associates with the RNA primase DnaG that synthesizes short RNA primers required for DNA synthesis at the lagging strand (Wu et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 1992

claim: DnaG synthesizes short RNA primers required for DNA synthesis at the lagging strand.
source: The helicase DnaB separates the two DNA strands (Mok and Marians, 1987) and transiently associates with the RNA primase DnaG that synthesizes short RNA primers required for DNA synthesis at the lagging strand (Wu et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 1992

claim: The clamp loader subcomplex loads the DNA sliding clamp β onto the DNA.
source: The clamp loader subcomplex (δ, δ', γ, τ, χ, ψ) loads the DNA sliding clamp β, the processivity factor for the DNA polymerase, onto the DNA (Stukenberg et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stukenberg et al., 1991

claim: The clamp loader connects the leading and lagging strand polymerases via its τ subunits.
source: It furthermore connects the leading and lagging strand polymerases via its τ subunits (McHenry, 1982; Onrust et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to McHenry, 1982 and Onrust et al., 1995

claim: The activity of PolIIIα is poor in isolation.
source: The activity of PolIIIα is poor in isolation (Maki and Kornberg, 1985) and is greatly enhanced by its associated proteins.
evidence: Supported by citation to Maki and Kornberg, 1985

claim: The exonuclease ε removes misincorporated bases.
source: For error-free DNA synthesis the polymerase relies on the exonuclease ε that removes any misincorporated bases and decreases the error rate of DNA replication by 1–2 orders of magnitude (Scheuermann et al., 1983; Lancy et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Scheuermann et al., 1983 and Lancy et al., 1989

claim: The exonuclease ε decreases the error rate of DNA replication by 1-2 orders of magnitude.
source: For error-free DNA synthesis the polymerase relies on the exonuclease ε that removes any misincorporated bases and decreases the error rate of DNA replication by 1–2 orders of magnitude (Scheuermann et al., 1983; Lancy et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Scheuermann et al., 1983 and Lancy et al., 1989

claim: The exonuclease strengthens the interactions between the polymerase and clamp by binding both proteins simultaneously.
source: In addition, the exonuclease strengthens the interactions between the polymerase and clamp as it binds both proteins simultaneously (Toste Rêgo et al., 2013; Jergic et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Toste Rêgo et al., 2013 and Jergic et al., 2013

claim: At the leading strand, the PolIIIα-clamp interaction is stable and results in DNA segments of >100,000 bp synthesized per binding event.
source: At the leading strand this interaction is stable and results in DNA segments of >100.000 bp synthesized per binding event (Yao et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yao et al., 2009

claim: At the lagging strand, DNA synthesis is discontinuous with an average length of 1000 bp synthesized per fragment.
source: At the lagging strand in contrast, DNA synthesis is discontinuous, with an averaged length of 1000 bp synthesized per fragment, depending on the frequency of the RNA primase activity (Wu, Zechner and Marians, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu, Zechner and Marians, 1992

claim: The C-terminal domain of τ (τc) acts as a 'processivity switch' for the polymerase to enable repeated binding and release at the lagging strand.
source: Finally, the C-terminal domain of τ (τc) acts as a 'processivity switch' for the polymerase to enable repeated binding and release at the lagging strand (Leu et al., 2003; Georgescu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Leu et al., 2003 and Georgescu et al., 2009

claim: The structures of the helicase-primase subcomplex have been known for some time.
source: The structures of the helicase-primase subcomplex (Bailey et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2008) and the clamp loader subcomplex (Jeruzalmi et al., 2001; Simonetta et al., 2009) have been known for some time.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bailey et al., 2007 and Wang et al., 2008

claim: The structures of the clamp loader subcomplex have been known for some time.
source: The structures of the helicase-primase subcomplex (Bailey et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2008) and the clamp loader subcomplex (Jeruzalmi et al., 2001; Simonetta et al., 2009) have been known for some time.
evidence: Supported by citations to Jeruzalmi et al., 2001 and Simonetta et al., 2009

claim: The structure of the PolIIIα-clamp-exonuclease-τc complex has remained elusive due to its dynamic nature.
source: The structure of the PolIIIα-clamp-exonuclease-τc complex on the other hand has remained elusive due to its dynamic nature that forms a significant hurdle for structure determination.
evidence: Stated as a known challenge in the field

claim: The cryo-EM structures of the PolIIIα-clamp-exonuclease-τ500 complex were determined to 8 Å resolution in both DNA-bound and DNA-free states.
source: To overcome this, we have used a combination of site directed mutagenesis and computational classification of different structural states to determine the cryo-EM structures of the complex in both a DNA-bound and a DNA-free state to 8 Å resolution.
evidence: Reported as the primary result of this study

claim: The interaction between PolIIIα and the clamp is weak, in the order of 1 μM.
source: The interaction between PolIIIα and the clamp is weak, in the order of 1 μM (Toste Rêgo et al., 2013), and is not sufficient to maintain an intact complex at the low concentrations used for cryo-EM.
evidence: Supported by citation to Toste Rêgo et al., 2013

claim: Sequences derived from the translesion DNA polymerase UmuC and the DNA replication initiation factor Hda were the most potent inhibitors of the interaction between the polymerase and clamp out of a panel of 15 peptide sequences.
source: For this we used sequences derived from the translesion DNA polymerase UmuC and the DNA replication initiation factor Hda that out of a panel of 15 peptide sequences were the most potent inhibitors of the interaction between the polymerase and clamp (Wijffels et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wijffels et al., 2004

claim: The stabilized complex is >100 fold more stable than the wild-type complex.
source: The obtained complex is >100 fold more stable than the wild-type complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Three structurally distinct groups of particles were identified from a single data set of 63,215 particles.
source: Three structurally distinct groups of particles could be identified from a single data set (63,215 particles).
evidence: Reported as a result of the cryo-EM data processing

claim: Two of the particle groups represent the PolIIIα-clamp-exonuclease-τ500 with and without DNA bound.
source: Two of these represent the PolIIIα-clamp-exonuclease-τ500 with and without DNA bound (Figure 1, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Reported as a result of the cryo-EM data processing, shown in Figure 1 and Videos 1 and 2

claim: The DNA-bound structure was refined to 8.0 Å resolution from 5663 particles.
source: The DNA-bound (5663 particles) and DNA-free (16,970 particles) structures were refined to 8.0 and 8.3 Å resolution, respectively
evidence: Reported as a result of the cryo-EM refinement

claim: The DNA-free structure was refined to 8.3 Å resolution from 16,970 particles.
source: The DNA-bound (5663 particles) and DNA-free (16,970 particles) structures were refined to 8.0 and 8.3 Å resolution, respectively
evidence: Reported as a result of the cryo-EM refinement

claim: The third class contains DNA but the tail domain of the polymerase and τ500 are not visible due to structural heterogeneity.
source: The third class contains DNA too, but in this complex the tail domain of the polymerase and τ500 are not visible due to structural heterogeneity.
evidence: Reported as an observation from the cryo-EM data processing

claim: The 'DNA-bound, no tail' structure was refined to 7.3 Å resolution from 40,582 particles.
source: The remaining particles (40,582) were classified into the third class in which the tail domain is not visible. Due to the larger number of particles, this structure was refined to 7.3 Å resolution.
evidence: Reported as a result of the cryo-EM refinement

claim: The overall conformation of PolIIIα resembles that of the X-ray structure of E. coli and Taq PolIIIα.
source: The overall conformation of PolIIIα resembles that of the X-ray structure of E. coli and Taq PolIIIα (Lamers et al., 2006; Bailey et al., 2006)
evidence: Comparison with crystal structures cited from Lamers et al., 2006 and Bailey et al., 2006

claim: There is a ~15° rotation of the fingers domain between the cryo-EM structure and the X-ray structures.
source: The overall conformation of PolIIIα resembles that of the X-ray structure of E. coli and Taq PolIIIα (Lamers et al., 2006; Bailey et al., 2006) and reveals only a ∼15° rotation of the fingers domain between the two structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Reported as a result of structural comparison, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: PolIIIα interacts with the clamp through the internal clamp binding motif (residues 920-924).
source: PolIIIα interacts with the clamp through the internal clamp binding motif (residues 920–924) (Dohrmann and McHenry, 2005; Toste Rêgo et al., 2013) that binds in the canonical binding pocket of the clamp (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dohrmann and McHenry, 2005 and Toste Rêgo et al., 2013, and shown in Figure 2B

claim: The region of the polymerase immediately after the clamp binding motif (approximately residues 927-936) is flexible.
source: Immediately after the clamp binding motif the density for the polymerase disappears, and resumes ∼10 residues later, just before the oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide binding (OB) domain, indicating that this region of the polymerase is flexible (Figure 2A, left and middle panel).
evidence: Inferred from the absence of density in the cryo-EM map

claim: The PHP domain of the polymerase comes close to but makes no contacts with the clamp.
source: On the other side of the complex, across the opening of the clamp, the PHP domain of the polymerase comes close to, but makes no contacts with the clamp (Figure 2A, left panel).
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2A

claim: The exonuclease is wedged between the clamp and the thumb domain of PolIIIα.
source: Instead, the exonuclease is wedged between the clamp and the thumb domain of PolIIIα (Figure 2A, right panel).
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2A

claim: The catalytic domain of the exonuclease is in direct contact with the polymerase thumb domain.
source: The catalytic domain of the exonuclease is in direct contact with the polymerase thumb domain whereas the contact with the clamp is mediated via a canonical clamp binding motif that is located immediately downstream of the catalytic domain (Toste Rêgo et al., 2013; Jergic et al., 2013).
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure and supported by citations to Toste Rêgo et al., 2013 and Jergic et al., 2013

claim: Both pockets of the dimeric clamp are occupied in the ternary complex.
source: This clamp binding motif is bound to the pocket of the clamp in a manner similar to the polymerase in the other half of the clamp (cf. Figure 2B,C) and hence both pockets of the dimeric clamp are occupied in the ternary complex.
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figures 2B and 2C

claim: A stretch of approximately 15 residues in the exonuclease tail is disordered.
source: Downstream of the clamp binding motif the tail of the exonuclease follows the contours of the polymerase PHP domain, where it is disordered for a stretch of ∼15 residues that were shown to be mobile by NMR (Ozawa et al., 2013).
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure and supported by NMR data cited from Ozawa et al., 2013

claim: The C-terminal helix of the exonuclease packs tightly against the PHP domain of PolIIIα.
source: Finally, the C-terminal helix of the exonuclease that mediates most of the binding to the polymerase (Ozawa et al., 2013) packs tightly against the PHP domain of PolIIIα (Figure 2A, left and right panel), similar to the crystal structure of the PolIIIα-PHP domain and C-terminal helix of the exonuclease (Ozawa et al., 2013).
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure and consistent with crystal structure cited from Ozawa et al., 2013

claim: In the ternary complex the exonuclease simultaneously binds the polymerase and clamp.
source: Hence, in the ternary complex the exonuclease simultaneously binds the polymerase and clamp.
evidence: Inferred from the observed contacts in the cryo-EM structure

claim: The exonuclease strengthens the association between the polymerase and clamp, which is required for processive DNA synthesis.
source: By doing so it strengthens the association between the two proteins (Toste Rêgo et al., 2013), which is required for processive DNA synthesis (Jergic et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Toste Rêgo et al., 2013 and Jergic et al., 2013

claim: The cryo-EM model shows an improved fit of cross-links compared to the previous model based on cross-linking data alone.
source: When we map the same cross-links onto the cryo-EM model we find an improved fit of the cross-links with the model, due to the conformational changes in the complex as well as the detailed information about the interactions between the proteins that could not be modeled based on the cross-links alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Comparison of cross-linking data with the cryo-EM model shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The NMR structure of residues 500-621 of τ can be fitted into the density between the tail and fingers domain of the polymerase.
source: The NMR structure of residues 500–621 of τ (Su et al., 2007) can be fitted into the density between the tail and fingers domain of the polymerase (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Fitting of NMR structure cited from Su et al., 2007 into the cryo-EM density

claim: The C-terminal end of τ is in contact with the tail of the polymerase.
source: The C-terminal end of τ is in contact with the tail of the polymerase.
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure

claim: The last 23 residues of τ that bind the polymerase are not part of the NMR structure.
source: Unfortunately, the last 23 residues of τ that bind the polymerase (Jergic et al., 2007) are not part of the NMR structure and are therefore not present in our model.
evidence: Stated limitation of the model based on the available NMR structure

claim: A second contact is found between the globular domain of τ500 and the fingers domain of the polymerase.
source: A second contact is found between the globular domain of τ500 and the fingers domain of the polymerase.
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure

claim: The contact between τ500 and the polymerase fingers domain is mediated by residues 530-535 and 562-566 of τ500 and residues 657-667 of PolIIIα.
source: This contact is mediated by residues 530–535 and 562–566 of τ500 and residues 657–667 of PolIIIα (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: The position of τ500 in the E. coli complex is different from the position of the C-terminal domain of τ in complex with Taq PolIIIα.
source: The position of τ500 in this complex is different from the position of the C-terminal domain of τ in complex with Taq PolIIIα, where it is located at the opposite side of the polymerase tail (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: Comparison with structure cited from Liu et al., 2013, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: The C-terminal domain of τ from E. coli and Taq share no sequence or structural homology.
source: It must be noted though that the C-terminal domain of τ from E. coli and Taq share no sequence or structural homology and therefore engage with the polymerase in different ways.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: The entire length of the 25 base pair duplex is in contact with protein in the DNA-bound complex.
source: In the DNA-bound complex (Figure 3), the entire length of the 25 base pair duplex is in contact with protein (Figure 3A).
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3A

claim: The position of the DNA is similar to that of the DNA in the crystal structure of Taq PolIIIα and Geobacillus kaustophilus PolC.
source: The position of the DNA is similar to that of the DNA in the crystal structure of Taq PolIIIα and Geobacillus kaustophilus PolC (Wing et al., 2008; Evans et al., 2008) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Comparison with crystal structures cited from Wing et al., 2008 and Evans et al., 2008, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: No density is observed for the 4 nucleotide single stranded overhang on the template strand, indicating that this part of the DNA is flexible.
source: No density is observed for the 4 nucleotide (nt) single stranded overhang on the template strand indicating that this part of the DNA is flexible.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of density in the cryo-EM map

claim: All contacts to the DNA are mediated by the thumb, palm and fingers domains of the polymerase and the inner surface of the clamp.
source: In the complex, all contacts to the DNA are mediated by the thumb, palm and fingers domains of the polymerase and the inner surface of the clamp.
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure

claim: No contacts to the DNA are made by the polymerase OB domain, the exonuclease, or τ500.
source: No contacts to the DNA are made by the polymerase OB domain, the exonuclease, or τ500.
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure

claim: The most extensive DNA contacts occur at the primer 3' end in polymerase active site where the thumb, palm and fingers domain of the polymerase contact the first 9 base pairs of the DNA duplex.
source: The most extensive DNA contacts occur at the primer 3' end in polymerase active site where the thumb, palm and fingers domain of the polymerase contact the first 9 base pairs of the DNA duplex.
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure

claim: A loop of the thumb (residues 464-470) is inserted into the major groove of the DNA, making the only non-backbone contact.
source: It is also here that the only non-backbone contact is made by a loop of the thumb (residues 464–470), which is inserted into the major groove of the DNA (Figure 3B).
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3B

claim: The tip of the fingers domain makes additional contacts to the DNA away from the active site.
source: Away from the active site, the tip of the fingers domain (i.e. little finger [Lamers et al., 2006] or β binding domain [Bailey et al., 2006]), makes additional contacts to the DNA.
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure

claim: Several positively charged residues (K831, K872, R876, R877, K881) and the positive charge of the helix dipole of two helices (residues 842-856 and 875-886) are pointed towards the DNA backbone at the tip of the fingers domain.
source: Here, several positively charged residues (K831, K872, R876, R877, K881) as well as the positive charge of the helix dipole of two helices (residues 842–856 and 875–886) are pointed towards the DNA backbone (Figure 3A).
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3A

claim: The OB domain is in close proximity of the DNA but makes no contacts with it.
source: At this position, the OB domain is in close proximity of the DNA but makes no contacts with it (Figure 3C).
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3C

claim: The OB domain forms a bridge between the PolIIIα fingers domain, thumb domain, and the exonuclease.
source: Instead, the OB domain forms a bridge between the PolIIIα fingers domain, thumb domain, and the exonuclease.
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure

claim: The isolated OB domain has been shown to bind to ssDNA.
source: Furthermore, while the isolated OB domain has been shown to bind to ssDNA (Georgescu et al., 2009), in this complex the OB domain is ∼40 Å away from the ssDNA template.
evidence: Supported by citation to Georgescu et al., 2009

claim: In the complex, the OB domain is approximately 40 Å away from the ssDNA template.
source: Furthermore, while the isolated OB domain has been shown to bind to ssDNA (Georgescu et al., 2009), in this complex the OB domain is ∼40 Å away from the ssDNA template.
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure

claim: The DNA interacts with the clamp that surrounds the DNA like a nut around a bolt.
source: The DNA furthermore interacts with the clamp that surrounds the DNA like a nut around a bolt (Figure 3D).
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3D

claim: Several non-specific contacts are made to the backbone of the DNA providing an electrostatic cushion for the DNA to pass through.
source: Several non-specific contacts are made to the backbone of the DNA providing an electrostatic cushion for the DNA to pass through as it leaves the complex.
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure

claim: Compared to the crystal structure of the isolated clamp bound to DNA, the clamp is rotated by approximately 20°, resulting in an almost perpendicular orientation (approximately 80°) with respect to the DNA.
source: Compared to the crystal structure of the isolated clamp bound to DNA (Georgescu et al., 2008a) the clamp is rotated by ∼20°, resulting in an almost perpendicular orientation (∼80°) with respect to the DNA.
evidence: Comparison with crystal structure cited from Georgescu et al., 2008a

claim: In the 19 Å negative stain EM structure of Pyrococcus furiosus PolB, the DNA runs straight through the clamp.
source: In the 19 Å, negative stain EM structure of Pyrococcus furiosus PolB, the only other known structure of a DNA polymerase in complex with clamp and DNA, the DNA runs straight through the clamp as well (Mayanagi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mayanagi et al., 2011

claim: PolIIIα has DNA synthesis speeds of up to 600-1000 nt/s.
source: PolIIIα is an extremely fast DNA polymerase with DNA synthesis speeds of up to 600–1000 nt/s (Mok and Marians, 1987; Mcinerney et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mok and Marians, 1987 and Mcinerney et al., 2007

claim: E. coli Pol I has a synthesis speed of 15 nt/s.
source: In contrast, the E. coli DNA polymerases Pol I, Pol II, and Pol IV have synthesis speeds of 15, 10, and 1 nt/s, respectively (Schwartz and Quake, 2009; Indiani et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schwartz and Quake, 2009 and Indiani et al., 2009

claim: E. coli Pol II has a synthesis speed of 10 nt/s.
source: In contrast, the E. coli DNA polymerases Pol I, Pol II, and Pol IV have synthesis speeds of 15, 10, and 1 nt/s, respectively (Schwartz and Quake, 2009; Indiani et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schwartz and Quake, 2009 and Indiani et al., 2009

claim: E. coli Pol IV has a synthesis speed of 1 nt/s.
source: In contrast, the E. coli DNA polymerases Pol I, Pol II, and Pol IV have synthesis speeds of 15, 10, and 1 nt/s, respectively (Schwartz and Quake, 2009; Indiani et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schwartz and Quake, 2009 and Indiani et al., 2009

claim: In isolation, PolIIIα has a surprisingly low affinity for DNA when compared to the other E. coli DNA polymerases.
source: Furthermore, in isolation PolIIIα has a surprisingly low affinity for DNA when compared to the other E. coli DNA polymerase (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A

claim: PolIIIα has a uniquely long fingers domain that is more than twice as long as the other E. coli DNA polymerases.
source: To this effect, PolIIIα may have evolved its uniquely long fingers domain that is more than twice as long as the other E. coli DNA polymerases (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: In PolIIIα, the number of base pairs between the 3' end of the primer and the opening of the clamp is 22.
source: In PolIIIα, the number of base pairs between the 3' end of the primer and the opening of the clamp is 22, while the predicted number of base pairs for Pol I, Pol II, and Pol IV is ∼15.
evidence: Measured from the cryo-EM structure

claim: The predicted number of base pairs between the 3' end of the primer and the opening of the clamp for Pol I, Pol II, and Pol IV is approximately 15.
source: In PolIIIα, the number of base pairs between the 3' end of the primer and the opening of the clamp is 22, while the predicted number of base pairs for Pol I, Pol II, and Pol IV is ∼15.
evidence: Predicted from structural modeling

claim: PolIIIα is the only polymerase that inserts a loop of the thumb domain into the major groove of the DNA.
source: At the same time, the sequence-independent backbone contacts and the perfectly straight B-form DNA may facilitate the rapid exit of the DNA from the active site. The active site itself is wrapped tightly around the DNA where PolIIIα is the only polymerase that inserts a loop of the thumb domain into the major groove of the DNA, while the thumb domains of Pol I, Pol II, and Pol IV only have backbone contacts with the DNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C

claim: The thumb domains of Pol I, Pol II, and Pol IV only have backbone contacts with the DNA.
source: At the same time, the sequence-independent backbone contacts and the perfectly straight B-form DNA may facilitate the rapid exit of the DNA from the active site. The active site itself is wrapped tightly around the DNA where PolIIIα is the only polymerase that inserts a loop of the thumb domain into the major groove of the DNA, while the thumb domains of Pol I, Pol II, and Pol IV only have backbone contacts with the DNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C

claim: The combination of unique contacts with the DNA may have evolved to support the high speeds of DNA synthesis by PolIIIα without compromising accuracy.
source: Hence, it seems plausible that this combination of unique contacts with the DNA may have evolved to support the high speeds of DNA synthesis by PolIIIα without compromising accuracy.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the structural observations

claim: The complex undergoes extensive conformational changes from the DNA-free to the DNA-bound state.
source: To enable the many contacts with the DNA, the complex undergoes extensive conformational changes from the DNA-free to the DNA-bound state.
evidence: Observed by comparing the two cryo-EM structures

claim: There is a ~35° rotation of the polymerase tail and τ500 from the DNA-free to the DNA-bound state.
source: Most prominent is a ∼35° rotation of the polymerase tail and τ500, which move from a position over the polymerase active site to a position adjacent to the sliding clamp (Figures 1,4 and Video 3).
evidence: Observed by comparing the two cryo-EM structures shown in Figures 1, 4 and Video 3

claim: The tail of PolIIIα consists of the OB domain (residues 960-1071) and the C-terminal τ-binding domain (residues 1079-1160).
source: The tail of PolIIIα consists of the OB domain (residues 960–1071) and the C-terminal τ-binding domain (residues 1079–1160).
evidence: Stated as a structural definition

claim: The polymerase tail and τ500 together form a rigid structure that shows few changes between the DNA free and DNA bound structure.
source: Together with τ500 they form a rigid structure that shows few changes between the DNA free and DNA bound structure, indicating that the interaction between τ500 and the tail of PolIIIα must be stable (Figure 4C).
evidence: Observed by comparing the two cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 4C

claim: The interaction between τ500 and the tail of PolIIIα is stable.
source: Together with τ500 they form a rigid structure that shows few changes between the DNA free and DNA bound structure, indicating that the interaction between τ500 and the tail of PolIIIα must be stable (Figure 4C).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the structure shows few changes between states

claim: As a result of the repositioning of the polymerase tail, the contact between τ500 and the fingers domain of the polymerase is broken.
source: As a result of the repositioning of the polymerase tail, the contact between τ500 and the fingers domain of the polymerase is broken and a new contact between the OB domain and the clamp is forged (Figure 4B and Video 3).
evidence: Observed by comparing the two cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 4B and Video 3

claim: A new contact between the OB domain and the clamp is forged in the DNA-bound state.
source: As a result of the repositioning of the polymerase tail, the contact between τ500 and the fingers domain of the polymerase is broken and a new contact between the OB domain and the clamp is forged (Figure 4B and Video 3).
evidence: Observed in the DNA-bound cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4B and Video 3

claim: The OB domain makes two new contacts with the clamp via a short helix (1035-1043) and a long protruding loop (1003-1013).
source: The OB domain makes two new contacts with the clamp via a short helix (1035–1043) and a long protruding loop (1003–1013) (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Observed in the DNA-bound cryo-EM structure shown in Figures 4D and 4E

claim: The OB domain contacts the clamp at loops 24-28 and 275-278.
source: These motifs contact the clamp at loops 24–28 and 275–278, respectively.
evidence: Observed in the DNA-bound cryo-EM structure

claim: In the DNA-bound complex, the polymerase has three points of contact to the clamp: one via the canonical clamp binding motif (residues 920-925), one indirectly via the exonuclease, and one contact via the OB domain.
source: Hence in the DNA-bound complex, the polymerase has three points of contact to the clamp: one via the canonical clamp binding motif (residues 920–925: Figure 2B); one indirectly via the exonuclease (Figure 2C); and one contact via the OB domain (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Observed in the DNA-bound cryo-EM structure

claim: A triple mutation in OB domain (R1004S, K1009S, R1010S) results in reduced DNA synthesis.
source: Previously, it has been shown that a triple mutation in OB domain result in reduced DNA synthesis (Georgescu et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Georgescu et al., 2009

claim: The mutations R1004S, K1009S, R1010S are located at the interface between the OB domain and the clamp.
source: However, in our structure the OB domain is far away (∼40 Å) from the ssDNA overhang of the template strand. Instead, the mutations (R1004S, K1009S, R1010S) are located at the interface between the OB domain and the clamp (Figure 4E)
evidence: Observed in the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4E

claim: The mutations R1004S, K1009S, R1010S could weaken the interaction between the polymerase and clamp, providing an alternative explanation for the reduced DNA synthesis.
source: Instead, the mutations (R1004S, K1009S, R1010S) are located at the interface between the OB domain and the clamp (Figure 4E) and therefore could weaken the interaction between the polymerase and clamp, providing an alternative explanation for the reduced DNA synthesis.
evidence: Inferred from the location of the mutations in the cryo-EM structure

claim: The cryo-EM structures reveal the nature of the interactions in the ternary complex.
source: The cryo-EM structures of the PolIIIα-clamp-exonuclease-τ500 complex presented in this work finally reveal the nature of the interactions in the ternary complex and are a crucial step forward towards determining the structure of the complete bacterial replisome.
evidence: Summary of the main findings of the study

claim: The structures are a crucial step forward towards determining the structure of the complete bacterial replisome.
source: The cryo-EM structures of the PolIIIα-clamp-exonuclease-τ500 complex presented in this work finally reveal the nature of the interactions in the ternary complex and are a crucial step forward towards determining the structure of the complete bacterial replisome.
evidence: Stated as the significance of the work

claim: The structures show how the clamp and exonuclease tether the polymerase to the DNA through multiple contacts.
source: Our cryo-EM structures furthermore provide a crucial insight into the structural organization of the replicative DNA polymerase and its associated proteins clamp, exonuclease and τ500. They show how the clamp and exonuclease tether the polymerase to the DNA through multiple contacts.
evidence: Summary of structural observations from the cryo-EM data

claim: The structures reveal a large conformational change where the tail of the polymerase moves from interacting with the clamp in the DNA-bound state, to a position 35 Å away from the clamp in the DNA-free state.
source: Importantly, they also reveal a large conformational change where the tail of the polymerase moves from interacting with the clamp in the DNA-bound state, to a position 35 Å away from the clamp in the DNA-free state.
evidence: Observed by comparing the two cryo-EM structures

claim: On the lagging strand, the polymerase repositions to a newly primed site every approximately 1000 bp.
source: On the lagging strand, the polymerase repositions to a newly primed site every ∼1000 bp.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about lagging strand synthesis

claim: The polymerase needs to release both clamp and DNA to reposition on the lagging strand.
source: To do so, the polymerase needs to release both clamp and DNA.
evidence: Logical inference from the requirement to reposition

claim: The switch-like movement of the polymerase tail may play a part in the release and consequent repositioning of the polymerase at the end of the Okazaki fragment.
source: We propose that the switch-like movement of the polymerase tail may play a part in the release and consequent repositioning of the polymerase at the end of the Okazaki fragment.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on the structural observations

claim: During DNA synthesis, the tail of the polymerase is bound to the clamp, stabilizing the interaction between polymerase and clamp.
source: During DNA synthesis, the tail of the polymerase is bound to the clamp, stabilizing the interaction between polymerase and clamp (marked with '1' in Figure 5).
evidence: Proposed model based on the DNA-bound structure shown in Figure 5

claim: The DNA-bound conformation may be further stabilized by the presence of a DNA binding region immediately upstream of τ500.
source: This confirmation may be further stabilized by the presence of a DNA binding region immediately upstream of τ500 (marked with '2') (Jergic et al., 2007).
evidence: Proposed model based on data cited from Jergic et al., 2007

claim: Upon encounter of a release signal, τ500 rebinds to the polymerase fingers domain, sequestering the polymerase tail away from the clamp and initiating the dissociation of the polymerase from clamp and DNA.
source: Upon encounter of a release signal, τ500 rebind to the polymerase fingers domain (marked with '3') thus sequestering the polymerase tail away from the clamp (marked with '4') and initiating the dissociation of the polymerase from clamp and DNA.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on the structural observations

claim: In the 'collision' model, the encounter with the dsDNA of the previous Okazaki fragment induces the release of the polymerase.
source: Two non-exclusive models have been proposed (Li and Marians, 2000). In the 'collision' model, the encounter with the dsDNA of the previous Okazaki fragment induces the release of the polymerase.
evidence: Supported by citation to Li and Marians, 2000

claim: A decreasing gap size between the 3' terminus of the lagging strand and the 5' end of the previously synthesized Okazaki fragment promotes release of the polymerase.
source: In support of this model, it has been shown that a decreasing gap size between the 3' terminus of the lagging strand and the 5' end of the previously synthesized Okazaki fragment promotes release of the polymerase (Leu et al., 2003; Georgescu et al., 2009; Dohrmann et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Leu et al., 2003, Georgescu et al., 2009, and Dohrmann et al., 2011

claim: The ssDNA binding properties of the OB domain in the tail of the polymerase has been proposed to play a role in the sensing of the ssDNA vs dsDNA.
source: The ssDNA binding properties of the OB domain in the tail of the polymerase has been proposed to play a role in the sensing of the ssDNA vs dsDNA (Georgescu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Georgescu et al., 2009

claim: The C-terminal fragment of τ may act as the sensor for the decreasing gap size as it is required to release the polymerase from a decreasing gap size.
source: Alternatively, it has been proposed that the C-terminal fragment of τ may act as the sensor as it is required to release the polymerase from a decreasing gap size (Leu et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leu et al., 2003

claim: The region in τ immediately upstream of τ500 has DNA binding affinity.
source: Indeed, it was found that the region in τ, immediately upstream of τ500, has DNA binding affinity (Jergic et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jergic et al., 2007

claim: The release of the polymerase by a decreasing gap size is too slow (t1/2 = 110 s) for the frequency at which the lagging strand polymerase is re-positioned (every 1-2 s).
source: Contesting the collision model is the observation that the release of the polymerase by a decreasing gap size is too slow (t1/2 = 110 s) for the frequency at which the lagging strand polymerase is re-positioned (every 1–2 s) (Dohrmann et al., 2011), suggesting that additional or alternative release factors are required.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dohrmann et al., 2011

claim: The 'signaling' model proposes that the trigger comes from one of the other components of the replisome such as the RNA primase DnaG.
source: The alternative 'signaling' model therefore proposes that the trigger comes from one of the other components of the replisome such as the RNA primase DnaG, based on the observation that the increased primase concentration results in shorter lagging strand fragments (Wu, Zechner and Marians, 1992; Li and Marians, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu, Zechner and Marians, 1992 and Li and Marians, 2000

claim: Increased primase concentration results in shorter lagging strand fragments.
source: The alternative 'signaling' model therefore proposes that the trigger comes from one of the other components of the replisome such as the RNA primase DnaG, based on the observation that the increased primase concentration results in shorter lagging strand fragments (Wu, Zechner and Marians, 1992; Li and Marians, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu, Zechner and Marians, 1992 and Li and Marians, 2000

claim: The presence of a primer alone is sufficient to induce release at the lagging strand and activity of the primase is not required.
source: However, it was recently shown that the presence of a primer alone is sufficient to induce release at the lagging strand and that activity of the primase is not required (Yuan and McHenry, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yuan and McHenry, 2014

claim: The τ protein is both part of the clamp loader complex that positions clamps onto the primer and simultaneously binds the polymerase, making it a suitable conveyor of the signal.
source: Yet, the fact that the τ protein is both part of the clamp loader complex that positions clamps onto the primer and simultaneously binds the polymerase makes this a suitable conveyor of the signal.
evidence: Logical inference from known properties of τ

claim: Amino acid residues 920-924 of E. coli PolIIIα were changed from QADMF to QLDLF to increase binding to the clamp.
source: To increase binding to the clamp, amino acid residues 920–924 of E. coli PolIIIα were changed by site directed mutagenesis from QADMF to QLDLF, while in the exonuclease residues 182–187 were changed from QTSMAF to QLSLPL, based on sequences described in (Wijffels et al., 2004).
evidence: Described as a method used in the study

claim: In the exonuclease, residues 182-187 were changed from QTSMAF to QLSLPL to increase binding to the clamp.
source: To increase binding to the clamp, amino acid residues 920–924 of E. coli PolIIIα were changed by site directed mutagenesis from QADMF to QLDLF, while in the exonuclease residues 182–187 were changed from QTSMAF to QLSLPL, based on sequences described in (Wijffels et al., 2004).
evidence: Described as a method used in the study

claim: Data was collected using a Titan Krios electron microscope operated at 300 kV equipped with a K2 summit direct electron detector.
source: All data was collected using a Titan Krios electron microscope (FEI) operated at 300 kV equipped with a K2 summit direct electron detector (Gatan, Pleasaston, CA).
evidence: Described as a method used in the study

claim: Images were collected in single-electron counting mode at a calibrated magnification of 28.571x (1.76 Å/pixel).
source: Images were collected in single-electron counting mode at a calibrated magnification of 28.571x (1.76 Å/pixel), using a flux of 2 e/Å2/sec and a total dose of 40 e/Å2 over a total of 20 frames.
evidence: Described as a method used in the study

claim: A total of 1350 micrographs were recorded from which >550,000 particles were picked automatically.
source: A total of 1350 micrographs were recorded from which >550,000 particles were picked automatically in Relion.
evidence: Described as a result of the data collection

claim: After 2D classification, a dataset of approximately 90,000 particles was obtained.
source: After 2D classification, a large number of spurious particles as well as particles that show free polymerase or free clamp were removed, yielding a dataset of ∼90,000 particles.
evidence: Described as a result of the data processing

claim: The resolution of these reconstructions is limited by both the relatively small size of the complex (250 kDa) and the inherent flexibility of this four-protein and DNA complex.
source: We believe that the resolution of these reconstructions is limited by both the relatively small size of the complex (250 kDa), which hampers accurate alignment and classification, and the inherent flexibility of this four-protein and DNA complex.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the resolution limitations

claim: The maps are of excellent quality, with individual helices, β-sheets, and loops clearly visible.
source: Still, the maps are of excellent quality, with individual helices, β-sheets, and loops clearly visible in the map (Figure 1C).
evidence: Assessment of the cryo-EM map quality shown in Figure 1C

claim: The PolIIIα structure was divided into five domains that were fitted independently into density as rigid bodies.
source: The PolIIIα structure was divided into five domains that were further fitted independently into density as rigid bodies (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: Described as a method used in the study

claim: The five domains of PolIIIα are: PHP (residues 1-280), palm-fingers (residues 281-432 + 510-810), thumb (residues 433-509), tip-of-fingers (residues 811-928) and C-terminal tail (residues 929-1160).
source: These domains were: PHP (residues 1–280), palm-fingers (residues 281–432 + 510–810), thumb (residues 433–509), tip-of-fingers (residues 811–928) and C-terminal tail (residues 929–1160).
evidence: Described as a method used in the study
